```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
library(BayesianQDM)
```

This vignette describes the analysis of a proof-of-concept (PoC) study with
two binary endpoints (Yamaguchi et al., submitted).
`vignette("overview")` introduces the decision criteria for one endpoint.

## Model

The responses of a subject on the two endpoints fall into one of four cells,
`"00"`, `"01"`, `"10"` and `"11"`, where the first digit is the response on
endpoint 1 and the second the response on endpoint 2. In group $k$, the
counts $x_k$ of the four cells follow a multinomial distribution with cell
probabilities $p_k = (p_{k,00}, p_{k,01}, p_{k,10}, p_{k,11})$, which have a
Dirichlet prior distribution $\textrm{Dir}(\alpha_k)$ (`prior_dirichlet()`).
The posterior distribution is $\textrm{Dir}(\alpha_k + x_k)$, and with
external data $x_{e}$ borrowed with weight $a_0$ it is
$\textrm{Dir}(\alpha_k + a_0 x_{e} + x_k)$.

The response rates of the two endpoints are the margins
$\pi_{k1} = p_{k,10} + p_{k,11}$ and $\pi_{k2} = p_{k,01} + p_{k,11}$, and
the treatment effects are $\theta_j = \pi_{tj} - \pi_{cj}$ ($j = 1, 2$).

## Regions and criteria

The target values and minimum acceptable values divide the plane of
$(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ into nine regions:

```{r regions}
qdm_regions("posterior")
```

With `rule = "joint"` (the default), the Go criterion is that the posterior
probability of the union of `go_regions` is at least $\gamma_{go}$, and the
NoGo criterion that the probability of the union of `nogo_regions` is at
least $\gamma_{nogo}$. The defaults, region 1 for Go and region 9 for NoGo,
require both effects to exceed their target values and both to be at most
their minimum acceptable values. With `rule = "and"` or `rule = "or"`, the
criteria are applied to each endpoint separately and combined with AND or
OR.

For the predictive criterion, the null values divide the plane of the
future effects into four regions:

```{r regions-pred}
qdm_regions("predictive")
```

The posterior probabilities of the regions are estimated with `nMC` draws
from the Dirichlet posterior distributions. The predictive probabilities are
computed exactly from the joint distribution of the numbers of future
responders on the two endpoints.

## Decision for observed data

The first case study of Yamaguchi et al. (submitted) has 10 subjects per
group, $\textrm{Dir}(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25)$ priors,
$\theta_{TV} = (0.15, 0.15)$ and $\theta_{MAV} = (0.10, 0.10)$. Here the
thresholds are $\gamma_{go} = \gamma_{nogo} = 0.6$ (the article calibrates
its own thresholds), and `nMC = 2000` keeps the computations quick:

```{r design}
prior <- prior_dirichlet(rep(0.25, 4))
des <- design_binary2(
  n_t = 10, n_c = 10, prior_t = prior, prior_c = prior,
  criterion = criterion_posterior(theta_tv = c(0.15, 0.15),
                                  theta_mav = c(0.10, 0.10),
                                  gamma_go = 0.6, gamma_nogo = 0.6),
  nMC = 2000
)
dec <- qdm_decide(des, data_t = data_binary2(c(3, 2, 2, 3)),
                  data_c = data_binary2(c(6, 2, 1, 1)), seed = 1)
dec
```

The posterior probability of region 1 is
`r format(dec$prob_go, digits = 3)`, and the decision is `r dec$decision`.
With `rule = "and"`, the Go criterion requires each endpoint to meet its
threshold separately:

```{r and}
des_and <- design_binary2(
  n_t = 10, n_c = 10, prior_t = prior, prior_c = prior,
  criterion = criterion_posterior(theta_tv = c(0.15, 0.15),
                                  theta_mav = c(0.10, 0.10),
                                  gamma_go = 0.6, gamma_nogo = 0.6,
                                  rule = "and"),
  nMC = 2000
)
qdm_decide(des_and, data_t = data_binary2(c(3, 2, 2, 3)),
           data_c = data_binary2(c(6, 2, 1, 1)), seed = 1)
```

For the predictive criterion with 30 future subjects per group:

```{r predictive}
des_pred <- design_binary2(
  n_t = 10, n_c = 10, prior_t = prior, prior_c = prior,
  criterion = criterion_predictive(theta_null = c(0, 0), m_t = 30,
                                   gamma_go = 0.6, gamma_nogo = 0.6)
)
qdm_decide(des_pred, data_t = data_binary2(c(3, 2, 2, 3)),
           data_c = data_binary2(c(6, 2, 1, 1)))
```

## External data and hypothetical controls

External data of either group are given as cell counts and borrowed with a
power prior weight:

```{r external}
des_ext <- design_binary2(
  n_t = 10, n_c = 10, prior_t = prior, prior_c = prior,
  criterion = criterion_posterior(theta_tv = c(0.15, 0.15),
                                  theta_mav = c(0.10, 0.10),
                                  gamma_go = 0.6, gamma_nogo = 0.6),
  external_c = borrow(data_binary2(c(12, 3, 3, 2)), a0 = 0.5),
  nMC = 2000
)
qdm_decide(des_ext, data_t = data_binary2(c(3, 2, 2, 3)),
           data_c = data_binary2(c(6, 2, 1, 1)), seed = 1)$posterior_c
```

For a study without a concurrent control group, `hypothetical()` with cell
counts adds the hypothetical control data to the prior of the control group:

```{r hypothetical}
des_hyp <- design_binary2(
  n_t = 10, n_c = 0, prior_t = prior, prior_c = prior,
  criterion = criterion_posterior(theta_tv = c(0.15, 0.15),
                                  theta_mav = c(0.10, 0.10),
                                  gamma_go = 0.6, gamma_nogo = 0.6),
  hypothetical_c = hypothetical(data = data_binary2(c(6, 2, 1, 1))),
  nMC = 2000
)
qdm_decide(des_hyp, data_t = data_binary2(c(3, 2, 2, 3)), seed = 1)
```

With `fixed_c`, the control response rates of the two endpoints are known
values $(\pi_{c1,0}, \pi_{c2,0})$, for example those of the standard of care
reported in the literature. The effects are then
$\theta_j = \pi_{tj} - \pi_{cj,0}$, and `prior_c` must be `NULL`:

```{r fixed}
des_fix <- design_binary2(
  n_t = 10, n_c = 0, prior_t = prior,
  criterion = criterion_posterior(theta_tv = c(0.15, 0.15),
                                  theta_mav = c(0.10, 0.10),
                                  gamma_go = 0.6, gamma_nogo = 0.6),
  fixed_c = c(0.2, 0.2), nMC = 2000
)
qdm_decide(des_fix, data_t = data_binary2(c(3, 2, 2, 3)), seed = 1)
```

## Efficacy and safety endpoints

The favorable direction can differ between the endpoints. For an efficacy
endpoint (a response, on which larger effects are favorable) and a safety
endpoint (the occurrence of an adverse event, on which smaller effects are
favorable), `direction = c("greater", "less")` reverses the inequalities of
endpoint 2, so that region 1 is still the most favorable one:

```{r regions-safety}
qdm_regions("posterior", direction = c("greater", "less"))
```

Here the first digit of a cell is the response and the second the adverse
event. The decision is Go if, with probability at least 0.5, the response
rate is improved by more than 0.15 and the rate of the adverse event is
increased by less than 0.1 (region 1), and NoGo if, with probability at
least 0.6, the response rate is improved by at most 0.1 and the rate of the
adverse event is increased by at least 0.2 (region 9):

```{r safety}
des_safety <- design_binary2(
  n_t = 10, n_c = 10, prior_t = prior, prior_c = prior,
  criterion = criterion_posterior(theta_tv = c(0.15, 0.1),
                                  theta_mav = c(0.10, 0.2),
                                  gamma_go = 0.5, gamma_nogo = 0.6,
                                  direction = c("greater", "less")),
  nMC = 2000
)
qdm_decide(des_safety, data_t = data_binary2(c(2, 1, 5, 2)),
           data_c = data_binary2(c(6, 1, 2, 1)), seed = 1)
```

## Operating characteristics

A scenario gives the response rates of the two endpoints and their
correlation in each group. `cellprob_binary2()` converts them into the cell
probabilities; a correlation is feasible only if all four probabilities are
non-negative.

```{r cellprob}
cellprob_binary2(pi1 = 0.35, pi2 = 0.35, rho = 0.3)
```

By default (`enumerate = TRUE`), `qdm_oc()` enumerates all outcomes of the
study, `choose(n + 3, 3)` per group (`r choose(13, 3)` for 10 subjects), and
computes the region probabilities once for every pair of treatment and
control outcomes, with the same Monte Carlo draws for all pairs. The
computing time is proportional to the number of pairs times `nMC`; for large
sample sizes, `enumerate = FALSE` simulates `nsim` studies instead.

```{r oc}
effects <- expand.grid(theta1 = c(0, 0.15, 0.3), theta2 = c(0, 0.15, 0.3))
scen <- data.frame(pi_t1 = 0.2 + effects$theta1,
                   pi_t2 = 0.2 + effects$theta2, rho_t = 0.3,
                   pi_c1 = 0.2, pi_c2 = 0.2, rho_c = 0.3)
oc <- qdm_oc(des, scen, seed = 1)
oc
plot(oc)
```

A scenario whose correlation is outside the feasible range is not evaluable:
its probabilities are `NA`, with a warning, and it is marked "NE" in the
plot.

With `overlay = TRUE`, the decisions are drawn in a single heat map, as in
Figure 2 of Yamaguchi et al. (submitted): each cell has the color of the
decision with the highest probability, shaded in five steps of that
probability (below 0.5, 0.5 to 0.6, 0.6 to 0.7, 0.7 to 0.8, and 0.8 or
more). `cell_values = FALSE` leaves out the probabilities written in the
cells:

```{r oc-overlay}
plot(oc, overlay = TRUE)
plot(oc, overlay = TRUE, cell_values = FALSE)
```

The decision boundaries of `qdm_boundary()` (see `vignette("single-binary")`)
are not available for two binary endpoints, because the decision depends on
the four cell counts of the treatment group and cannot be shown on two axes.

## Calibration of the thresholds

With `rule = "joint"`, `qdm_calibrate()` chooses one threshold for the Go
criterion and one for the NoGo criterion. Here the Go criterion should be
met with probability at most 0.1 when neither endpoint is improved, and the
NoGo criterion with probability at most 0.2 when both effects are 0.3:

```{r calibrate}
cal <- qdm_calibrate(des, scenario_go = scen[1, ], scenario_nogo = scen[9, ],
                     target_go = 0.1, target_nogo = 0.2, seed = 1)
cal
plot(cal)
```

The calibrated thresholds add up to `r cal$gamma_go + cal$gamma_nogo`. When
the sum is 1 or less, a Go and a NoGo criterion can be met together (a Miss
decision); here Miss decisions have probability up to
`r format(max(cal$oc$Miss), digits = 2)` under the two scenarios, which the
warning reports. `qdm_calibrate()` chooses the smallest thresholds that meet
the targets, and larger thresholds also meet them, with more Gray decisions.
For example, the design with $\gamma_{go} = \gamma_{nogo} = 0.6$ used above
meets the Go criterion with probability `r format(oc$Go[1], digits = 2)`
when neither endpoint is improved and the NoGo criterion with probability
`r format(oc$NoGo[9], digits = 2)` when both effects are 0.3, and Miss
decisions are impossible because the thresholds add up to more than 1.

## Reference

Yamaguchi, Y., Hu, H., Huang, Y., Han, C., Homma, G. and Wang, A.
(submitted). Bivariate Bayesian quantitative decision-making for two
endpoints in rare disease drug development.
